passage: Urban planners in Medellín found that adding cable cars to hillside neighborhoods did not eliminate long commutes, but it did ______ them: average travel time to the city center fell by nearly half.
why: The commutes were not eliminated but got much better. Exacerbate is the opposite, and efface (erase) contradicts "did not eliminate."

passage: A 2019 review concluded that while the drug cannot cure the disease, it can ______ its symptoms enough for patients to return to work.
why: "Cannot cure, but" sets up partial improvement. Precipitate would bring symptoms on.

passage: Unlike her contemporaries, who filled their canvases with mythological scenes, painter Agnes Martin ______ recognizable subject matter altogether, working only with faint grids and bands of pale color.
why: "Unlike" plus "only grids and bands" means she deliberately avoided subject matter.

passage: Because the journal's editors wanted the findings to reach nonspecialists, they asked contributors to ______ technical jargon in favor of plain language.
why: "In favor of plain language" means jargon is to be avoided.

passage: Biographers have often ______ the composer's long silences in letters as evidence of depression; newly discovered diaries show that he simply wrote less when he was busiest.
why: The diaries show the biographers' reading was wrong, so they misinterpreted the silences.

passage: The author warns that readers who take the narrator's boasts at face value will ______ the novel, which is meant as a critique of exactly that kind of arrogance.
why: Taking a critique at face value is a wrong reading.

passage: Rather than offering a single theory of why the colony failed, the historian simply ______ the hardships its settlers faced: drought, crop disease, a harsh winter, and the loss of two supply ships.
why: A list follows the colon. The historian lists; she does not fix, avoid or misread.

passage: The treaty's third article ______ the specific rights retained by each nation, naming fishing access, river navigation, and mineral claims in turn.
why: "Naming ... in turn" is the definition of enumerate.

passage: Microplastics are now ______: researchers have detected them in Arctic snow, deep-sea sediment, and even human blood.
why: The examples show they are everywhere.

passage: Although the semicolon was once ______ in English prose, appearing several times per page in eighteenth-century novels, it is comparatively rare in fiction today.
why: "Several times per page" and the contrast with "rare" call for "everywhere." Anomalous would mean rare.

passage: The apparent link between the two variables proved ______: once the researchers controlled for household income, the relationship disappeared entirely.
why: A link that vanishes under a control was never real. Unequivocal and irrefutable say the opposite.

passage: Scholars now regard the letter as ______, noting that its paper was manufactured decades after its supposed author's death.
why: Paper made after the author died means the letter is a fake.

passage: The printing press did not immediately ______ hand copying; for decades, scribes and printers worked side by side, and some patrons continued to prefer manuscripts.
why: Working side by side means copying was not yet replaced. The press did supplement copying, so "did not supplement" contradicts the passage.

passage: In many Pacific Northwest estuaries, an invasive cordgrass has ______ native eelgrass, which now survives only in small patches.
why: The native grass has been pushed out and replaced.

passage: Most of the star's dimming events follow a regular 24-day cycle, so the ______ dip recorded in March, which lasted three times as long as any other, prompted astronomers to look for a second orbiting body.
why: The March dip breaks the regular pattern. Analogous would mean it resembled the others.

passage: The team initially dismissed the result as ______, but when four independent laboratories obtained the same unexpected value, it could no longer be treated as an outlier.
why: "Treated as an outlier" restates the blank.

passage: The mayor's habit of consulting residents before every major decision ______ a degree of public trust that her predecessors had never enjoyed.
why: Consulting residents produced trust. The other three would reduce or avoid it.

passage: Economists worried that the sudden price controls would ______ shortages, since producers would have little reason to supply goods at a loss.
why: The controls would cause shortages. "Worried" rules out ameliorate.

passage: Even the poet's earliest notebooks ______ the preoccupation with memory that would define her mature work.
why: The notebooks show the preoccupation. "Even the earliest" rules out avoiding or erasing it.

passage: Though the letters are formal in tone, they ______ genuine affection: the senator asks after each of his correspondent's children by name.
why: The detail after the colon is evidence of affection, so the letters reveal it.

passage: Dickinson's punctuation is famously ______: no other poet of her era used dashes and capital letters in quite the way she did.
why: "No other poet ... in quite the way she did" means it was hers alone.

passage: The dictionary's first editor relied on his own ______ system of filing, one so personal that after his death his successors needed two years to decipher it.
why: "His own" and "so personal" point to a system peculiar to him. An unequivocal system would have been easy to read.

passage: Rain and foot traffic have so thoroughly ______ the carvings on the temple steps that archaeologists must rely on nineteenth-century drawings to know what they depicted.
why: If drawings are needed to know what the carvings showed, the carvings have been worn away.

passage: The translator aimed to ______ herself from the text entirely, believing that readers should hear only the author's voice.
why: She wants to disappear from the text: to efface herself.

passage: The cheerful melody seems ______ with the song's lyrics, which describe the aftermath of a shipwreck.
why: A cheerful tune clashes with lyrics about a shipwreck.

passage: Visitors often remark on the ______ sight of a nineteenth-century lighthouse standing in the middle of a wheat field, miles from the nearest coast; the lake it once served dried up in the 1930s.
why: A lighthouse in a wheat field is out of place. It is real, so it is not spurious.

passage: Because ancient temperatures cannot be measured directly, climatologists use the ratio of oxygen isotopes in ice cores as a ______ for them.
why: The isotope ratio stands in for a quantity that cannot be measured directly.

passage: Unable to attend the vote, the councilor sent her deputy as her [[proxy]], with written instructions on how to cast her ballot.
why: Here it is the person sense: someone empowered to act for her. "Indirect measurement" is the data sense, which does not fit a deputy.

passage: The editor cut the final chapter, arguing that it was ______: every point it made had already been established earlier in the book.
why: A chapter that repeats what is already established is unnecessary, not false.

passage: Engineers found that the bridge's third support cable was not ______, as the original critics had claimed; without it, the span failed in every simulation of high winds.
why: The cable turned out to be needed, so it was not unnecessary.

passage: In her essay, the critic ______ the closing of the city's last independent bookstore, calling it "a loss that no online retailer can repair."
why: Calling it an irreparable loss is an expression of grief.

passage: While some linguists ______ the disappearance of regional dialects, others see the change as an ordinary and even healthy feature of living languages.
why: "While ... others see it as healthy" sets up the opposite attitude: regret.

passage: The scientist's paper ends with an ______: researchers who apply the new technique without first calibrating their instruments, she cautions, will produce meaningless results.
why: "She cautions" tells you the paper ends with a warning.

passage: Ignoring his mentor's ______ against publishing prematurely, the young chemist announced the discovery before anyone had replicated it.
why: A mentor's advice "against" doing something is a warning.

passage: Earlier trials had produced mixed results, but the latest study was ______: every one of the 400 participants who received the vaccine developed antibodies.
why: "Mixed results, but" calls for the opposite of mixed. Equivocal means mixed.

passage: The board's statement was far from ______; its vague wording left employees unsure whether the factory would close or merely reduce its hours.
why: Vague wording that leaves people unsure is far from clear.

passage: The sailor's account of the storm was long doubted, but logbooks recovered from two other ships in the area ______ it in nearly every detail.
why: "Long doubted, but" plus independent logbooks: the account is confirmed.

passage: A hypothesis based on a single fossil remains tentative until further finds ______ it.
why: More finds would supply the independent support that makes it less tentative.

passage: Although the emperor remained the ______ ruler of Japan throughout the Tokugawa period, actual authority rested with the shogun.
why: "Although ... actual authority rested with the shogun" means ruler in name only.

passage: The library lends tools to residents for a [[nominal]] charge, just enough to cover the cost of sharpening and repairs.
why: The charge is real, so "in name only" is wrong. "Just enough to cover" costs means token, very small.

passage: By setting the film in the house where she grew up, the director ______ even ordinary scenes with a sense of personal memory.
why: "Scenes with a sense of" fits the pattern imbue X with Y: she fills them with memory.

passage: The architect wanted to ______ the hospital with a feeling of calm, so she specified natural light, wood surfaces, and views of a garden from every room.
why: She wants the building filled with calm.

passage: Historians of medieval daily life face a ______ of sources: peasants left almost no written records, so much must be inferred from court documents and archaeology.
why: "Almost no written records" is a shortage. Myriad is the opposite.

passage: The region's ______ of pollinators has forced some orchard owners to fertilize blossoms by hand.
why: Fertilizing by hand is only necessary if pollinators are scarce.

passage: Contrary to the assumption that all screen time is ______ to children's development, the study found that certain interactive programs actually improved vocabulary.
why: "Contrary to" plus "actually improved" means the assumption was that screen time is harmful.

passage: Road salt keeps highways safe in winter, but its runoff is ______ to freshwater species, many of which cannot tolerate even small increases in salinity.
why: Species that cannot tolerate the salt are harmed by it.

passage: The bank's collapse did not create the region's economic weaknesses, but it did ______ the crisis, turning a slow decline into a sudden panic.
why: The collapse brought the crisis on suddenly: "slow decline into a sudden panic."

passage: The council later admitted that its [[precipitate]] vote, taken only an hour after the proposal was introduced, had left no time to consider the costs.
why: Adjective sense. A vote taken with no time to think is hasty, which is not the same as decisive.

passage: The grant's terms ______ that at least half of the funds be spent on equipment, leaving the lab little freedom to hire additional staff.
why: Terms set requirements. Speculate (guess) is the look-alike trap.

passage: The will ______ that the collection never be divided, so the museum had to accept all 3,000 objects or none.
why: The will imposed a binding condition.

passage: For many economists, the 1929 crash is the ______ financial panic, the case against which all later ones are measured.
why: "The case against which all later ones are measured" defines a model example.

passage: Far from being an oddity, the finch is a ______ example of adaptive radiation, cited in nearly every textbook to illustrate how one species diversifies into many.
why: "Far from an oddity" and "cited in nearly every textbook" point to the standard example.

passage: Wegener's theory of continental drift was ridiculed during his lifetime, but the discovery of seafloor spreading in the 1960s ______ him.
why: "Ridiculed ... but" a later discovery: he was proved right.

passage: The inspector's insistence on a second test, which colleagues had called excessive, was ______ when the retest revealed a crack the first had missed.
why: The retest showed the insistence was justified.

passage: The new solar cells ______ a property of perovskite crystals that silicon lacks: the ability to absorb light across nearly the entire visible spectrum.
why: The cells make use of a helpful property. Neutral sense.

passage: The memoir recounts the aviator's early [[exploits]], including a solo crossing of the Andes in an open-cockpit biplane.
why: Noun sense: a solo crossing of the Andes is a daring feat.

passage: Although she published three well-regarded novels, they have been ______ by her single book of essays, which remains the only work of hers most readers know.
why: The essays overshadow the novels.

passage: By 1910, petroleum had [[eclipsed]] whale oil as a source of lamp fuel.
why: Figurative sense: petroleum overtook whale oil. Nothing is literally hidden or darkened.

passage: Early drafts of the proposal were ______, a loose collection of goals with no timeline, budget, or assigned responsibilities.
why: "A loose collection ... with no timeline" describes something without structure.

passage: Unlike quartz, whose atoms are arranged in a repeating lattice, glass is ______: its atoms have no long-range order.
why: "No long-range order" is the technical meaning of amorphous.

passage: The defense conceded that the fingerprint evidence was ______ and shifted its argument to the question of motive.
why: If the defense concedes the evidence and changes the subject, it could not be disproved.

passage: The mathematician cautioned that a pattern holding for the first million cases, however suggestive, is not ______ proof; only a formal demonstration can rule out a later exception.
why: A pattern that might still meet an exception has not been proved beyond dispute.

passage: The octopus's ______ defenses include camouflage, ink clouds, jet propulsion, and the ability to detach an arm.
why: Four different kinds of defense are listed.

passage: No single cause explains the empire's decline; historians point instead to ______ pressures, from currency debasement to plague to frontier wars.
why: "No single cause" and three unlike examples mean many different kinds.

passage: A longtime ______ of public transit, the senator has voted for every rail funding bill introduced during her tenure.
why: Voting for every rail bill makes her a supporter.

passage: ______ of the four-day workweek cite studies showing that productivity holds steady, while critics counter that those studies examined only office jobs.
why: They cite favorable studies and are contrasted with "critics," so they are supporters.

passage: Though personally committed to abolishing the tax, the governor took a ______ approach, proposing a modest reduction that she knew the legislature would actually pass.
why: She set aside her ideal for what would actually pass. Dogmatic would mean insisting on abolition.

passage: The engineers' choice of steel over carbon fiber was ______ rather than ideal: steel was heavier, but it was available immediately and local crews knew how to weld it.
why: "Rather than ideal" plus practical reasons.

passage: Thick forest canopy ______ the wind so effectively that air near the ground can be almost still even during a storm.
why: Still air under the canopy means the wind has been weakened.

passage: The vaccine uses an ______ form of the virus, one weakened enough that it cannot cause illness but can still provoke an immune response.
why: "One weakened enough" restates the blank.

passage: The smell of smoke was ______, clinging to every room of the house weeks after the fire.
why: "Every room" means it had spread throughout.

passage: The belief that lightning never strikes the same place twice is ______ despite being false: surveys find that a majority of adults accept it.
why: Held by a majority means widespread. "Despite being false" rules out irrefutable.

passage: A changing magnetic field ______ an electric current in a nearby wire, the principle behind every generator.
why: The field causes the current. Deduce is the look-alike.

passage: No offer of money could [[induce]] the farmer to sell the land his family had worked for six generations.
why: With a person as the object, induce means persuade. "Force" is too strong: an offer is not coercion.

passage: The inspector's review was ______: he glanced at the first page of the report, signed it, and moved on without visiting the site.
why: A glance and a signature is a minimal effort. Exhaustive and scrupulous are opposites.

passage: Critics complained that the film's apology scene felt ______, as if the screenwriter had included it only because audiences expected one.
why: Included only because it was expected: done without real care.

passage: Darwin took ______ notes during the voyage, filling more than a dozen notebooks with observations of geology and wildlife.
why: More than a dozen notebooks is a large amount.

passage: The region's ______ rainfall, more than four meters a year, supports one of the densest forests on Earth.
why: The figure given is about quantity: a great deal of rain.

passage: To keep the survey short, the researchers removed all ______ questions, retaining only those that bore directly on the hypothesis.
why: The kept questions "bore directly on the hypothesis," so the removed ones were irrelevant.

passage: The laboratory is shielded so that ______ vibrations from passing traffic cannot disturb the instruments.
why: Vibrations from traffic come from outside the experiment.

passage: To ______ the limited data from ground stations, the team added measurements from weather balloons and satellites.
why: They "added" to the data, so the ground data was increased, not replaced.

passage: Many orchestral musicians ______ their salaries by giving private lessons.
why: Lessons add to their income.

passage: The author ______ her central claim with data from three decades of census records.
why: Data offered for a claim supports it.

passage: Rather than ______ the theory, the new measurements exposed a flaw in one of its core assumptions.
why: "Rather than" sets up the opposite of exposing a flaw: strengthening.

passage: Critics charged that the company's 90-page privacy policy was written to ______ rather than inform, burying its key terms in dense legal language.
why: "Rather than inform" and "burying" point to deliberately making it unclear.

passage: Good scientific writing clarifies; jargon used for its own sake merely ______.
why: The semicolon contrasts clarifying with its opposite.

passage: For a small island nation, the loss of its fishing grounds would be ______ to economic collapse.
why: Losing the fishing grounds would amount to collapse. "Detrimental to collapse" would mean it harmed the collapse.

passage: The judge ruled that the company's silence was ______ to an admission, since it had been given three chances to deny the charge.
why: Silence after three chances counts as an admission.

passage: The plot is so ______, with flashbacks nested inside other flashbacks, that many viewers need a second viewing to follow it.
why: Nested flashbacks that need a second viewing are hard to follow.

passage: Simplifying the ______ application process, which had required eleven forms and three interviews, doubled the number of applicants.
why: A process that needed simplifying, with eleven forms, was overcomplicated. It had plenty of structure, so it was not amorphous.

passage: Physicists have struggled for a century to ______ general relativity with quantum mechanics, two theories that each work superbly but contradict each other at very small scales.
why: Two theories that contradict each other need to be made consistent.

passage: After the drought's third year, most farmers had [[reconciled]] themselves to smaller harvests and began planting hardier, lower-yield crops.
why: "Reconciled themselves to" means accepted something unwelcome.

passage: Planting trees along the riverbank will not prevent flooding, but it can ______ the damage by slowing the water and holding soil in place.
why: "Will not prevent, but" means the damage is lessened.

passage: To ______ the risk of data loss, the archive stores three copies of every file in separate locations.
why: Extra copies reduce the risk.

passage: The male bird's bright red plumage makes it ______ to predators, a cost that biologists believe is offset by its appeal to mates.
why: Bright red feathers make the bird easy for predators to see.

passage: The report is thorough on costs but contains one ______ omission: it never mentions who will pay them.
why: An obvious gap in an otherwise thorough report stands out.

passage: Her methods were hardly ______: at a time when most chemists worked alone, she ran her laboratory as a collective and published every paper under a shared name.
why: She did the opposite of what most chemists did, so her methods were hardly conventional.

passage: The economist's early papers accepted the ______ view that markets correct themselves; only later did he break with the mainstream.
why: "Break with the mainstream" tells you the earlier view was the mainstream one.

passage: The catalog is ______, listing every one of the painter's 2,100 known works along with its date, dimensions, and ownership history.
why: "Every one of" means complete. Exhausting (tiring) is the look-alike.

passage: After an ______ search of the archive, covering every box from 1840 to 1900, the historian concluded that the letter had never been filed there.
why: "Covering every box" is a complete search.

passage: The publication of the photographs ______ a public debate that lawmakers had avoided for years.
why: The photographs set a long-avoided debate in motion.

passage: Cheap sensors have ______ the growth of citizen science, allowing thousands of volunteers to collect air-quality data that once required expensive laboratory equipment.
why: The sensors made the growth happen faster.

passage: Historians sometimes pose ______ questions, asking, for example, how the war might have unfolded had the telegram never been intercepted.
why: "How it might have unfolded had ... never" is a what-if question.

passage: To estimate the policy's effect, economists must construct a ______: a model of what employment would have been had the law never passed.
why: "What employment would have been had the law never passed" defines the word.

passage: Where earlier histories of the railroad celebrated its financiers, Chang's account ______ the experiences of the Chinese laborers who built it.
why: "Where earlier histories celebrated financiers" sets up a shift of emphasis to the laborers.

passage: The exhibit's design [[foregrounds]] the artist's sketches, placing them at the entrance while the finished paintings hang in a side room.
why: The sketches get the best position, so they are being emphasized.

passage: With its neon sign, chrome counter, and bottomless coffee, the restaurant is the ______ American diner.
why: It has every typical feature, so it is the classic example.

passage: Critics call the novel the ______ work of the movement, the one book that displays every trait the school is known for.
why: "Displays every trait" makes it the most typical example.

passage: Once fossils of the same species were found on both continents, the claim that the two landmasses had always been separate became ______.
why: The fossils undercut the claim, so it could no longer be defended. Irrefutable is the opposite.

passage: Rising rents made the theater's position ______: within a year it could no longer cover its lease and was forced to close.
why: A situation that ends in forced closure could not be sustained.

passage: Despite its ______ size, barely five centimeters long, the pygmy seahorse has a remarkably complex courtship ritual.
why: "Barely five centimeters" is tiny, and "despite" contrasts size with complexity.

passage: The ______ hummingbird weighs less than a coin, yet it migrates more than 3,000 kilometers each year.
why: "Weighs less than a coin" tells you it is very small.

passage: The review ______ its praise for the film's visuals with criticism of its thin plot.
why: Praise balanced by criticism is moderated praise. Pattern: temper X with Y.

passage: The committee's optimism about the new drug was [[tempered]] by the small size of the trial.
why: A small trial is a reason for caution, so the optimism was toned down. "Hardened" is the metalworking sense.

passage: Ecologists regard the early disappearance of amphibians from a wetland as a ______ of broader collapse, since frogs and salamanders are unusually sensitive to pollution.
why: The sensitive species disappear first, signaling what is coming.

passage: The small, experimental exhibition of 1905 proved to be a ______ of the revolution in painting that followed over the next decade.
why: It came first and pointed to what followed.

passage: The team waited two days for the storm to ______ before attempting the summit.
why: You wait for a storm to die down.

passage: Public interest in the trial showed no sign of ______; if anything, attendance grew each week.
why: "If anything, attendance grew" means interest was not dying down. "No sign of mounting" would contradict the growth.

passage: Before the auction, an expert was hired to ______ the manuscript, which she valued at roughly two million dollars.
why: "She valued it at" restates the blank. Apprise means inform.

passage: The committee's task is to ______ each proposal on its scientific merit alone, without regard to the applicant's reputation.
why: Judging proposals on merit is evaluating them.

passage: The distance to the nearest star once seemed an ______ barrier to study, but spectroscopy allowed astronomers to analyze starlight without leaving Earth.
why: "Once seemed ... but" a way around was found: the barrier had looked impossible to overcome.

passage: Engineers had considered the mountain range ______ until a surveyor identified a pass low enough for a rail line.
why: "Until" a pass was found, the range seemed impossible to cross.

passage: The company chose not to lay anyone off, shrinking its workforce instead through ______: employees who retired or resigned were simply not replaced.
why: Not replacing people who leave is gradual reduction.

passage: The long siege became a contest of ______, each side hoping the other would run out of supplies first.
why: Each side is trying to outlast the other as supplies wear down.

passage: The survey's open-ended questions were designed to ______ detailed responses rather than simple yes-or-no answers.
why: Questions draw out responses.

passage: The comedian's deadpan delivery ______ laughter even from audiences who did not share her language.
why: Her delivery drew laughter out of the audience.

passage: A ______ editor, Ruiz checked every quotation in the manuscript against its original source.
why: Checking every quotation against its source is painstaking care.

passage: The accountant was ______ about separating the charity's funds from her own, keeping distinct ledgers and refusing even to borrow a stamp.
why: Refusing even a stamp shows extreme care to do right.

passage: Applicants must navigate a ______ approval process involving nine agencies, each with its own forms and deadlines.
why: Nine agencies with separate forms is an overcomplicated system.

passage: The tax code has grown so ______ that even professional preparers disagree about how its provisions interact.
why: If experts cannot agree on how it works, it is excessively complicated.

passage: In her later buildings, the architect ______ decoration to function, stripping away any element that did not serve a structural purpose.
why: Decoration was ranked below function.

passage: The narrator claims to treat his clerks as equals, yet he refers to them throughout as his [[subordinates]].
why: Noun sense. "Yet" contrasts "equals" with people ranked beneath him.

passage: The dark frame ______ the painting's bright colors, making them appear even more vivid.
why: "Even more vivid" means the colors are made more noticeable. Attenuate would dull them.

passage: The drought ______ existing inequalities: farmers with wells survived, while those who depended on rain lost everything.
why: The gap between the two groups widened. The other three all mean it shrank.

passage: The flow of electric current through a wire is ______ to the flow of water through a pipe: voltage plays the role of pressure, and resistance the role of a narrowing.
why: The second half maps one system onto the other, which is an analogy.

passage: The wings of bats and the wings of insects are ______ structures: they perform the same function but evolved independently.
why: Same function, separate origins: the biological definition of analogous.

passage: The difference between the two measurements, less than one part in a million, is ______ for most engineering purposes.
why: One part in a million is too small to matter.

passage: What seemed an ______ clerical error, a single misplaced decimal, ultimately cost the agency a $125 million spacecraft.
why: "What seemed ... ultimately cost" sets up something that looked trivial and was not.

passage: The disease may lie dormant for years before symptoms ______.
why: After dormancy, symptoms appear. They cannot abate before they exist.

passage: The reviewer called the paper's central calculation a [[manifest]] error, one that any reader with a calculator could spot.
why: Adjective sense. An error anyone could spot is obvious.

passage: Coral reefs shelter ______ species, by some estimates a quarter of all marine life.
why: A quarter of all marine life is a huge number of species.

passage: The city's water system faces a ______ of problems, including aging pipes, lead contamination, shrinking budgets, and a declining customer base.
why: A long list of problems is a great many. Dearth is the opposite.

passage: To ______ residents' fears about the new reactor, the utility opened the plant for public tours and published its safety data online.
why: Tours and open data are meant to calm fears.

passage: The apology did little to ______ the workers' anger, which only grew when they learned that executives had received bonuses.
why: "Did little to ... which only grew": the anger was not eased.

passage: Reviewers found the film's happy ending ______: a long-lost uncle appears in the final scene to pay off every debt.
why: A conveniently timed rich uncle is a forced, artificial device.

passage: The dialogue feels natural rather than ______, as though the playwright had simply recorded conversations overheard on a train.
why: "Natural rather than" calls for the opposite of natural.

passage: When the verdict was announced, the relief in the courtroom was ______: people exhaled, embraced, and wept.
why: Visible, physical reactions show a feeling you could almost touch.

passage: There was a ______ tension between the two researchers, evident to everyone at the conference even though neither said a word to the other.
why: "Evident to everyone" without a word spoken: the tension could be felt.

passage: Until recently, the ______ cost of genome sequencing, once nearly $100 million per person, kept it out of ordinary medical practice.
why: A cost that "kept it out of" practice was too high to allow it. Nominal means tiny.

passage: Shipping fresh fruit by air is technically possible but economically ______ for most growers, who rely on slower refrigerated ships instead.
why: "Possible but" too expensive to do.

passage: Scholars once ______ the painting to Rembrandt, but analysis of its pigments suggests it was made by one of his students.
why: The painting was credited to Rembrandt.

passage: The author ______ the town's decline to the closing of the mill, though records show that the population had been falling for a decade before.
why: The author names the mill as the cause.

passage: The ______ with which later physicists regarded Newton was so great that for a century few dared to question his theory of light.
why: Respect so deep that nobody dared question him.

passage: In many cultures, elders are treated with ______, consulted on every major decision and seated in places of honor.
why: Places of honor and constant consultation show deep respect.

passage: The statue's ______ expression, neither clearly smiling nor frowning, has invited centuries of competing interpretations.
why: An expression nobody can pin down is mysterious.

passage: The poet remains an ______ figure: she gave no interviews, left no letters, and published under three different names.
why: With no interviews or letters, she is hard to know.

passage: The final chapter does not introduce new evidence; it merely ______ the arguments made earlier in the book.
why: Nothing new, only a restatement of what came before. Capitulate means surrender.

passage: Before taking questions, the speaker briefly ______ her three main findings for those who had arrived late.
why: A brief restatement for latecomers is a recap.

passage: Late in life, the novelist ______ his early work, refusing to allow it to be reprinted and calling it "the mistakes of a young man."
why: Refusing reprints and calling it a mistake is disowning it.

passage: The new government ______ the treaty signed by its predecessor, declaring that it would honor none of its terms.
why: Honoring none of the terms is outright rejection.

passage: The reporter could not ______ the rumor: none of the three officials she contacted would confirm it, and no documents supported it.
why: No confirmation and no documents means no evidence for it.

passage: Claims on the label must be ______ by clinical trials before the product can be sold.
why: Trials supply the evidence behind the claims.

passage: The inspection was a ______; the official's real purpose was to learn which workers had spoken to reporters.
why: "Real purpose" signals that the stated one was a cover.

passage: Under the ______ of protecting public health, the council banned the street vendors, whose real offense was competing with established restaurants.
why: "Real offense" shows that public health was the excuse.

passage: The typesetter accidentally ______ two digits, so the pamphlet gave the year as 1789 instead of 1798.
why: 89 and 98 are the same digits swapped.

passage: The director ______ the play from Renaissance Verona to 1950s New York, keeping the plot but changing the setting entirely.
why: Same plot, moved into a different setting.

passage: In the diagram, solid arrows ______ the flow of energy, while dashed arrows indicate the flow of information.
why: Parallel with "indicate": the arrows stand for energy flow.

passage: The Greek letter sigma is used to ______ a sum.
why: A symbol stands for a meaning.

passage: Only with the new telescope could astronomers ______ the faint ring, which had been invisible in earlier images.
why: Something faint and previously invisible can now be made out.

passage: Even experienced tasters find it difficult to ______ any difference between the two varieties.
why: Detecting a subtle difference is discerning it.

passage: From the growth rates measured over five years, the researchers ______ that the forest would need another century to recover fully.
why: They extended five years of data to a hundred-year estimate.

passage: The author cautions against ______ from a single city's experience to the nation as a whole.
why: Going from one city to the whole country extends beyond the data.

passage: The senator set aside her prepared text and delivered ______ remarks, responding directly to what the previous speaker had said.
why: Setting aside the prepared text means speaking unrehearsed. Extraneous is the look-alike.

passage: Jazz prizes ______ invention: soloists are expected to compose new melodies on the spot.
why: "On the spot" means improvised.

passage: The judge ruled that the witness's opinion of the defendant's character was ______ to the question of whether the contract had been signed.
why: Character has no bearing on whether a signature exists.

passage: Whether the vase was made in 1740 or 1760 is [[immaterial]], the curator argues; what matters is that it is the only surviving example of the technique.
why: "What matters is" shows the date is irrelevant. A vase plainly has physical substance.

passage: The 2019 guidelines ______ all earlier versions, which should no longer be consulted.
why: If the old versions should no longer be used, the new ones replace them.

passage: Digital maps have largely ______ printed atlases, though some travelers still carry paper as a backup.
why: The newer technology has taken the older one's place.

passage: From childhood, Ramanujan showed a remarkable ______ for numbers, filling notebooks with formulas before he had any formal training.
why: A natural pull toward numbers, before any training.

passage: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because hemoglobin has a far greater [[affinity]] for it than for oxygen.
why: Chemistry sense: molecules bind; they do not feel fondness. Greater binding with carbon monoxide is what crowds out oxygen.

passage: Because testing the drug on humans was not yet permitted, researchers used cultured cells as a ______ for living tissue.
why: The cells stand in for tissue that cannot be tested.

passage: For orphaned chicks, a hand puppet shaped like an adult crane serves as a ______ parent, teaching them to feed without becoming attached to humans.
why: The puppet is a stand-in parent.

passage: The treaty ______ the border between the two countries, specifying its course river by river and ridge by ridge.
why: Specifying a border's course in detail is marking it out precisely.

passage: The opening chapter clearly ______ the scope of the study, stating which decades and regions it covers and which it leaves out.
why: Saying exactly what is in and out draws the boundaries of the study.

passage: The candidate's promises remained ______: she spoke of "renewal" and "a fresh start" without naming a single policy.
why: Slogans with no policy behind them are vague.

passage: What began as a ______ idea, little more than a hunch, became a precise hypothesis after two years of fieldwork.
why: A hunch, contrasted with "a precise hypothesis," is a hazy idea.

passage: The trial's results were ______: the drug helped some patients, harmed a few, and had no measurable effect on most.
why: Results pointing in three directions are inconclusive. Unequivocal is the opposite.

passage: Asked whether he would run again, the mayor gave an ______ answer that supporters and opponents alike interpreted as favoring their side.
why: An answer both sides can read their own way is ambiguous.

passage: To become a citizen of the new republic, the prince had to ______ his title and all claims to the throne.
why: He gives up what was his. Denounce (condemn) is the look-alike.

passage: After the scandal, the scientist ______ her earlier position, conceding publicly that the data did not support it.
why: Publicly conceding and abandoning a position she had held.

passage: The fossil's poor preservation ______ any firm conclusion about the animal's diet, since its teeth and stomach contents did not survive.
why: Without teeth or stomach contents, a firm conclusion is ruled out.

passage: Accepting the award does not ______ applying for other grants; recipients are free to seek additional funding.
why: "Free to seek" more funding means the award does not rule that out.

passage: Detected at an ______ stage, when only a few leaves show spots, the fungus can be stopped before it spreads through the orchard.
why: "Only a few leaves" and "before it spreads" describe the very start.

passage: The 1760s letters reveal an ______ sense of national identity, not yet fully formed but clearly emerging.
why: "Not yet fully formed but clearly emerging" defines the word.

passage: The poem's simple vocabulary ______ its complexity: beneath the plain words lies an intricate pattern of allusion.
why: The plain surface gives a false impression of what lies beneath.

passage: Her calm voice ______ the anxiety she later admitted feeling throughout the speech.
why: A calm voice hid real anxiety. Evinced would mean the calm voice revealed the anxiety, which is contradictory.

passage: Geologists long [[discounted]] reports of rocks falling from the sky, treating them as folklore until a well-witnessed meteorite shower in 1803.
why: "Treating them as folklore" shows the reports were dismissed.

passage: The reviewer cautions readers not to ______ the study merely because its sample was small, noting that its methods were unusually rigorous.
why: The warning is against dismissing a study for a weak reason.

passage: The seismograph [[registered]] a faint tremor several minutes before residents felt anything.
why: An instrument detects and records a reading.

passage: The warning was printed on every label, yet surveys showed it had not [[registered]] with most customers.
why: "Printed on every label, yet" means it was there but did not sink in.
